page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question
Classification of Elements – Periodic Properties · 2 marks

steps.label: The definitions
lines: Covalent radius: half the distance between
the nuclei of two like atoms joined by a
van der Waals radius: half the distance
between the nuclei of two nearest non-bonded
atoms of neighbouring molecules in the solid
steps.why: Both radii are half of a measured nucleus-to-nucleus distance; the difference is only whether the two atoms are bonded (covalent) or merely touching as neighbours (van der Waals).
common_mistakes: Leaving out single bond in the covalent radius. Double and triple bonds give shorter distances.
Defining the van der Waals radius between bonded atoms. It is measured between non-bonded neighbours.
steps.memory_tip: Both are half a distance: between bonded atoms for covalent, between touching neighbours for van der Waals.
steps.margin_note: The words bonded and non-bonded are what separate the two definitions.

steps.label: The comparison

lines.text: van der Waals radius > covalent radius

lines: A covalent bond pulls the two atoms into
overlap of their orbitals, while non-bonded
steps.why: Bonding shortens the measured distance because the atoms overlap; without a bond the full outer clouds keep the nuclei farther apart, so the van der Waals half-distance is always the larger one.
common_mistakes: Answering the comparison without a reason. The overlap of bonded atoms is the reason.
Writing the chlorine values swapped. The larger value, 1.80 Å, is the van der Waals radius.
steps.memory_tip: A bond pulls the atoms closer together, so the bonded (covalent) radius is the smaller of the two.
steps.margin_note: The chlorine pair 0.99 Å against 1.80 Å is the standard numerical illustration.
